Let’s Get Relevant!

Here we will clean up the data, then only select the data from June 2023 to August 2026, the month after the CDC’s official declaration of the end of COVID.

#add state column
metro_states = strsplit(housing$cbsa_title, ", ")
metro_states = unlist(metro_states)
states = metro_states[seq(2,length(metro_states),2)]
state = substring(states,1,2)
housing$state_ss = state # it counts DC as a state so there are 51

#cbsa_title and cbsa_code are factors
housing[,3] = as.factor(housing[,3])
housing[,2] = as.factor(housing[,2])

# add a month and a year column
housing$month_mm = housing[,1]%%100
housing$year_yyyy = housing[,1]%/%100

# date reformat and time constraint 
housing[,1] = as.Date(paste(housing[,1],"01"),'%Y%m%d')
postCOVID_housing = housing[housing$month_date_yyyymm > "2023-05-01",]

#house rank, state, month, and year are factors
postCOVID_housing[,4] = as.factor(postCOVID_housing[,4]) # rank
postCOVID_housing[,48] = as.factor(postCOVID_housing[,48]) # state
postCOVID_housing[,49] = as.factor(postCOVID_housing[,49]) # month
postCOVID_housing[,50] = as.factor(postCOVID_housing[,50]) # year

#make sure its quality
quality_housing = subset(postCOVID_housing, quality_flag==0)
str(quality_housing)

A little bit about our data set

This data set is from Realtor.com which is described on the website as a, “Residential Real Estate Data Library [that] is based on the extensive Realtor.com database of MLS-listed for-sale homes,” (Realtor.Com Real Estate Data and Market Trends for Download, n.d.). Since this data is collected from only MLS-listed for-sale homes only licensed real estate professionals can input listings directly. There are ways to pay a flat fee to add one’s house to the MLS but that is usually goes through, “licensed brokers who charge a one-time fee to post your listing on the local MLS,” (Haddad, 2026).

Looking on Realtor.com it has data visualizations of their data studying the markets, there are also different MLS reports that exist outside Realtor.com’s, but most of the reports on Realtor.com are summary statistics and just report on counts over time. No deeper analysis into relationships between variables within the website alone.

Looking at our numerical variables we noticed large ranges within variables like pending_listing_count and price increase/reduction count, so shifting to ratio data or share data gave us more normalized comparisons, and led us to think of 4 questions that we wanted to explore further.

What’s SMART About the Data?

Let’s explore our SMART Questions!

Data Preparation for Questions 1 and 2

Questions 1 and 2 compare each metro’s median listing price in June 2023 with its price in August 2026. We keep only those two months, place each metro in a size tier using its June 2023 household rank, and calculate one price change per metro.

housing_start <- quality_housing %>%
  dplyr::filter(year_yyyy == 2023, month_mm == 06) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(HouseholdRank, cbsa_code) %>%
  dplyr::transmute(
    cbsa_code,
    cbsa_title,
    HouseholdRank,
    price_2023 = median_listing_price,
    pending_2023 = pending_ratio,
    metro_size_group = factor(
      dplyr::ntile(HouseholdRank, 4),
      levels = 1:4,
      labels = c(
        "Tier 1 (Largest)",
        "Tier 2 (Upper-Mid)",
        "Tier 3 (Lower-Mid)",
        "Tier 4 (Smallest)"
      )
    )
  )

housing_end <- quality_housing %>%
  dplyr::filter(year_yyyy == 2026, month_mm == 08) %>%
  dplyr::transmute(
    cbsa_code,
    price_2026 = median_listing_price,
    pending_2026 = pending_ratio
  )

# One row per metro with both endpoints.
metro_endpoints <- housing_start %>%
  dplyr::inner_join(housing_end, by = "cbsa_code") %>%
  dplyr::filter(
    is.finite(price_2023),
    is.finite(price_2026),
    price_2023 > 0,
    price_2026 > 0
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    price_change_pct = 100 * (price_2026 - price_2023) / price_2023,
    log_price_change = log(price_2026 / price_2023)
  )

nrow(metro_endpoints)
## [1] 730

Question 1

After COVID (from June 2023 to August 2026), did the average change in median listing price differ across the four metro-size tiers?

EDA

It’s important to see the variation in our data before constructing our hypotheses. So let’s first plot the percent change in median listing price across all metros.

q1 <- subset(
  metro_endpoints,
  is.finite(log_price_change) &
  !is.na(metro_size_group)
)

stopifnot(anyDuplicated(q1$cbsa_code) == 0)

table(q1$metro_size_group)
## 
##   Tier 1 (Largest) Tier 2 (Upper-Mid) Tier 3 (Lower-Mid)  Tier 4 (Smallest) 
##                195                194                182                159
q1_colors <- c("blue", "lightblue", "gold", "orange")

ggplot(data = q1, aes(price_change_pct)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30,
                 col = "black",
                 fill = "blue",
                 alpha = .7) + # opacity
  labs(x = "% change in median listing price", y = "Frequency") +
  labs(title = "Histogram of % listing-price change post COVID")

qqnorm(q1$price_change_pct, main = "Q-Q plot of % Listing-Price Change post COVID")
qqline(q1$price_change_pct)


A percent change can’t fall below -100% but has no upper limit, so percent changes tend to be right skewed. So let’s log transform our data, using \(\log(\text{price}_{2026} / \text{price}_{2023})\), then plot again. For small changes the log change is close to the percent change (a log change of 0.10 is about 10.5%).

ggplot(data = q1, aes(log_price_change)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30,
                 col = "black",
                 fill = "blue",
                 alpha = .7) + # opacity
  labs(x = "log(price 2026 / price 2023)", y = "Frequency") +
  labs(title = "Histogram of log listing-price change post COVID")

ggplot(q1, aes(x = metro_size_group, y = log_price_change, fill = metro_size_group)) +
  geom_boxplot(colour = "black", outlier.colour = "red", outlier.shape = 2, outlier.size = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 4, colour = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = q1_colors) +
  labs(title = "Boxplot of metro-size tier vs log listing-price change post COVID",
       x = "Metro-size tier", y = "log(price 2026 / price 2023)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

q1_qq_plot <- ggplot(q1, aes(sample = log_price_change, color = metro_size_group)) +
  stat_qq(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ metro_size_group, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = q1_colors) +
  labs(title = "Q-Q plots of log listing-price change by tier post COVID",
       x = "Theoretical normal quantiles",
       y = "Log price-change quantiles") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

q1_qq_plot

q1_summary <- q1 %>%
  dplyr::group_by(metro_size_group) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    n = dplyr::n(),
    mean_log_change = mean(log_price_change),
    median_log_change = median(log_price_change),
    sd_log_change = sd(log_price_change),
    avg_pct_change = 100 * (exp(mean(log_price_change)) - 1)
  )

xkabledply(as.data.frame(q1_summary), title = "Log listing-price change by metro-size tier")
Log listing-price change by metro-size tier
metro_size_group n mean_log_change median_log_change sd_log_change avg_pct_change
Tier 1 (Largest) 195 -0.0359 -0.0432 0.0958 -3.53
Tier 2 (Upper-Mid) 194 0.0353 0.0298 0.1096 3.59
Tier 3 (Lower-Mid) 182 0.0542 0.0439 0.1415 5.57
Tier 4 (Smallest) 159 0.0809 0.0653 0.1470 8.42


In the boxplot, black diamonds show the mean of each tier and the lines inside the boxes show the median. The Q-Q plots show the log price changes are roughly normal in all four tiers. Tiers 2 and 3 have a longer upper tail, meaning a few metros had unusually large price gains, but with this many metros per tier the ANOVA holds up well to mild non-normality. So we can conduct an ANOVA test on log listing-price change.

Null Hypothesis Construction Metro-Size Tier

Null Hypothesis \(H_0: \mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3=\mu_4\) average log listing-price change is equal across all four metro-size tiers
Alternative Hypothesis \(H_1:\) at least one tier’s average log listing-price change is different
Alpha \(\alpha=0.05\)

ANOVA Hypothesis Testing Metro-Size Tier

q1_anova <- aov(log_price_change ~ metro_size_group, data = q1)
q1_pval <- summary(q1_anova)[[1]][1, 5]
xkabledply(q1_anova, title = "Log Listing-Price Change and Metro-Size Tier ANOVA result summary")
Log Listing-Price Change and Metro-Size Tier ANOVA result summary
Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
metro_size_group 3 1.37 0.4564 29.8 0
Residuals 726 11.14 0.0153 NA NA 
# Mean log change per tier, converted to average % change.
q1_means <- tapply(q1$log_price_change, q1$metro_size_group, mean)
q1_pct <- 100 * (exp(q1_means) - 1)
round(q1_pct, 2)
##   Tier 1 (Largest) Tier 2 (Upper-Mid) Tier 3 (Lower-Mid)  Tier 4 (Smallest) 
##              -3.53               3.59               5.57               8.42
# Check: Welch's ANOVA does not assume the tiers have equal spreads.
q1_welch_pval <- oneway.test(log_price_change ~ metro_size_group, data = q1, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value
q1_welch_pval
## [1] 2.22e-20

Analysis Metro-Size Tier


Our p-value is <0.001, which is below our \(\alpha\) (0.05), so we reject our null hypothesis and have data that supports our alternative hypothesis that average log listing-price change is not equal across all four metro-size tiers.

Converted to percentages, Tier 4 (Smallest) had the largest average price change (8.4%) and Tier 1 (Largest) had the smallest (-3.5%). Because the tiers have different spreads, we also ran Welch’s ANOVA, which gives a p-value of <0.001 and leads to the same conclusion.

Post-hoc Tukey Time for Metro-Size Tier

q1_tukey <- TukeyHSD(q1_anova)
q1_tukey
##   Tukey multiple comparisons of means
##     95% family-wise confidence level
## 
## Fit: aov(formula = log_price_change ~ metro_size_group, data = q1)
## 
## $metro_size_group
##                                         diff      lwr    upr p adj
## Tier 2 (Upper-Mid)-Tier 1 (Largest)   0.0712  0.03884 0.1035 0.000
## Tier 3 (Lower-Mid)-Tier 1 (Largest)   0.0901  0.05723 0.1230 0.000
## Tier 4 (Smallest)-Tier 1 (Largest)    0.1167  0.08266 0.1508 0.000
## Tier 3 (Lower-Mid)-Tier 2 (Upper-Mid) 0.0189 -0.01399 0.0518 0.450
## Tier 4 (Smallest)-Tier 2 (Upper-Mid)  0.0456  0.01144 0.0797 0.003
## Tier 4 (Smallest)-Tier 3 (Lower-Mid)  0.0266 -0.00798 0.0613 0.196
q1_tukey_table <- as.data.frame(q1_tukey$metro_size_group)
q1_sig_pairs <- rownames(q1_tukey_table)[q1_tukey_table$`p adj` < 0.05]


Each row compares two tiers, and pairs with a p adj below 0.05 have significantly different average log price changes. Significantly different pairs: Tier 2 (Upper-Mid)-Tier 1 (Largest); Tier 3 (Lower-Mid)-Tier 1 (Largest); Tier 4 (Smallest)-Tier 1 (Largest); Tier 4 (Smallest)-Tier 2 (Upper-Mid).

Question 2

After COVID (from June 2023 to August 2026), were increases in pending ratios associated with changes in median listing prices across metro areas?

Pending Ratio: The number of pending listings divided by the number of active listings. It measures the balance between supply (active listings) and demand (pending listings).
- Increase in Pending Ratio: The market got tighter. Demand grew relative to supply, meaning buyers faced more competition and sellers gained more leverage.
- Decrease in Pending Ratio: The market got looser. Supply grew relative to demand, meaning buyers gained more leverage and sellers faced more competition to sell.

We answer this two ways. An ANOVA compares the size of the average log price change between metros whose pending ratio increased and metros whose pending ratio decreased. A chi-square test compares the direction, meaning the share of metros whose listing price increased.

EDA

Let’s first group each metro by the direction of its pending ratio and its listing price. A metro counts as “Increased” if its August 2026 value is higher than its June 2023 value, and “Decreased” otherwise, so “Decreased” also includes the few metros with no change.

q2 <- subset(
  metro_endpoints,
  is.finite(log_price_change) &
  is.finite(pending_2023) &
  is.finite(pending_2026) &
  pending_2023 >= 0 &
  pending_2026 >= 0
)

stopifnot(nrow(q2) > 0)
stopifnot(anyDuplicated(q2$cbsa_code) == 0)

q2$pending_change <- q2$pending_2026 - q2$pending_2023

directions <- c("Increased", "Decreased")

q2$pending_group <- factor(
  ifelse(q2$pending_change > 0, "Increased", "Decreased"),
  levels = directions
)

q2$price_group <- factor(
  ifelse(q2$price_2026 > q2$price_2023, "Increased", "Decreased"),
  levels = directions
)

q2_colors <- c("Increased" = "#eb6834", "Decreased" = "#2a78d6")

table(q2$pending_group)
## 
## Increased Decreased 
##        81       647
table(q2$price_group)
## 
## Increased Decreased 
##       414       314


Next, let’s look at the spread of log listing-price change in each pending-ratio group.

ggplot(q2, aes(x = pending_group, y = log_price_change, fill = pending_group)) +
  geom_boxplot(colour = "black", outlier.colour = "red", outlier.shape = 2, outlier.size = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 4, colour = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = q2_colors) +
  labs(title = "Boxplot of pending-ratio direction vs log listing-price change post COVID",
       x = "Change in pending ratio", y = "log(price 2026 / price 2023)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

q2_qq_plot <- ggplot(q2, aes(sample = log_price_change, color = pending_group)) +
  stat_qq(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ pending_group, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = q2_colors) +
  labs(title = "Q-Q plots of log listing-price change by pending-ratio direction",
       x = "Theoretical normal quantiles",
       y = "Log price-change quantiles") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

q2_qq_plot

Finally, let’s count how many metros fall into each combination of pending-ratio direction and listing-price direction, and show each group’s split as a 100% stacked bar.

q2_table <- table(
  q2$pending_group,
  q2$price_group,
  dnn = c("Pending ratio", "Listing price")
)

addmargins(q2_table)
##              Listing price
## Pending ratio Increased Decreased Sum
##     Increased        55        26  81
##     Decreased       359       288 647
##     Sum             414       314 728
q2_prop <- 100 * prop.table(q2_table, margin = 1)

q2_bar <- as.data.frame(q2_prop)
names(q2_bar) <- c("pending_group", "price_group", "percent")
q2_bar$label <- ifelse(q2_bar$percent > 0, paste0(round(q2_bar$percent, 1), "%"), "")

q2_axis_labels <- paste0(directions, "\nn = ", rowSums(q2_table))

q2_plot <- ggplot(q2_bar, aes(pending_group, percent, fill = price_group)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = q2_colors, name = "Median listing-price change") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = q2_axis_labels) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 20), labels = paste0(seq(0, 100, 20), "%")) +
  labs(title = "Listing-price direction by pending-ratio direction post COVID",
       x = "Change in pending ratio",
       y = "Percentage of metros",
       caption = "'Decreased' includes unchanged values.") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

q2_plot

Null Hypothesis Construction Pending-Ratio Direction

Null Hypothesis \(H_0: \mu_{increased}=\mu_{decreased}\) average log listing-price change is equal for metros whose pending ratio increased and metros whose pending ratio decreased
Alternative Hypothesis \(H_1: \mu_{increased}\neq\mu_{decreased}\) average log listing-price change is different between the two groups
Alpha \(\alpha=0.05\)

ANOVA Hypothesis Testing Pending-Ratio Direction

q2_anova <- aov(log_price_change ~ pending_group, data = q2)
q2_pval <- summary(q2_anova)[[1]][1, 5]
xkabledply(q2_anova, title = "Log Listing-Price Change and Pending-Ratio Direction ANOVA result summary")
Log Listing-Price Change and Pending-Ratio Direction ANOVA result summary
Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
pending_group 1 0.0693 0.0693 4.05 0.0446
Residuals 726 12.4331 0.0171 NA NA 
# Mean log change per group, converted to average % change.
q2_means <- tapply(q2$log_price_change, q2$pending_group, mean)
q2_pct <- 100 * (exp(q2_means) - 1)
round(q2_pct, 2)
## Increased Decreased 
##      6.01      2.78
# Check: Welch's ANOVA does not assume the groups have equal spreads.
q2_welch_pval <- oneway.test(log_price_change ~ pending_group, data = q2, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value
q2_welch_pval
## [1] 0.0554

Analysis Pending-Ratio Direction


Our p-value is 0.0446, which is below our \(\alpha\) (0.05), so we reject our null hypothesis and have data that supports our alternative hypothesis that average log listing-price change is different between metros whose pending ratio increased and metros whose pending ratio decreased.

Converted to percentages, metros whose pending ratio increased had an average price change of 6%, compared with 2.8% for metros whose pending ratio decreased. Welch’s ANOVA gives a p-value of 0.0554 and leads to a different conclusion, so this result should be interpreted with caution. With only two groups, no post-hoc Tukey test is needed.

Null Hypothesis Construction Pending-Ratio Direction

Null Hypothesis \(H_0:\) pending-ratio direction and listing-price direction are independent
Alternative Hypothesis \(H_1:\) pending-ratio direction and listing-price direction are NOT independent
Alpha \(\alpha=0.05\)

\(\chi^2\) Hypothesis Testing Pending-Ratio Direction

# Expected counts if the two directions were independent.
q2_expected <- outer(rowSums(q2_table), colSums(q2_table)) / sum(q2_table)
dimnames(q2_expected) <- dimnames(q2_table)
round(q2_expected, 2)
##              Listing price
## Pending ratio Increased Decreased
##     Increased      46.1      34.9
##     Decreased     367.9     279.1
# Classroom rule: every expected count must be at least 5.
stopifnot(all(q2_expected >= 5))

q2_chi <- chisq.test(q2_table, correct = FALSE)
q2_chi_pval <- q2_chi$p.value
q2_chi
## 
##  Pearson's Chi-squared test
## 
## data:  q2_table
## X-squared = 5, df = 1, p-value = 0.03

Analysis Pending-Ratio Direction


All expected counts are at least 5, so the chi-square test is valid. Our p-value is 0.0334, which is below our \(\alpha\) (0.05), so we reject our null hypothesis and have data that supports our alternative hypothesis that pending-ratio direction and listing-price direction are associated.

67.9% of metros whose pending ratio increased saw their median listing price rise, compared with 55.5% of metros whose pending ratio decreased.

Both tests assume each metro is an independent observation, and they show association, not cause and effect.

Question 3a

After COVID (from June 2023 to August 2026) is the average number of price reduction/increase share the same across different metro areas, across states?
price_increased_share: The percent of houses that had price increases in that metro area
price_reduced_share: The percent of houses that had price reductions in that metro area

EDA

It’s important to see the variation in our data before constructing our hypotheses. So let’s plot the variation in price increase and reduce share.

ggplot(data=quality_housing, aes(price_increased_share)) + 
  geom_histogram(breaks=seq(0, 0.1, by = 0.002), 
                 col="green", 
                 fill="blue", 
                 alpha = .7) + # opacity
  labs(x="Price Increase Share", y="Frequency") +
  labs(title="Histogram of Price Increase Share Post COVID")

ggplot(data=quality_housing, aes(price_reduced_share)) + 
  geom_histogram(breaks=seq(0, 0.4, by = 0.02), 
                 col="yellow", 
                 fill="red", 
                 alpha = .7) + # opacity
  labs(x="Price Reduced Share", y="Frequency") +
  labs(title="Histogram of Price Reduced Share Post COVID")

qqnorm(quality_housing$price_increased_share, main="Q-Q plot of Price Increase Share post COVID")
qqline(quality_housing$price_increased_share)

qqnorm(quality_housing$price_reduced_share, main="Q-Q plot of Price Reduced Share post COVID")
qqline(quality_housing$price_reduced_share)


Reductions looks good but price_increase_shares is right skewed so lets normalize our data then plot again.

#log transform our data
log_housing = quality_housing
log_housing$log_inc_share = log10(log_housing$price_increased_share + 1)

ggplot(data=log_housing, aes(log_inc_share)) + 
  geom_histogram(breaks=seq(0, 0.1, by = 0.002), 
                 col="green", 
                 fill="blue", 
                 alpha = .7) + # opacity
  labs(x="log10(increase_share)", y="Frequency") +
  labs(title="Histogram of log price increase share post COVID")

qqnorm(log_housing$log_inc_share, main="Q-Q plot of log Price Increase Share post COVID")
qqline(log_housing$log_inc_share)


Our reduction histogram looks normal but the increase share even after normalizing is still skewed due to the large amount of 0s so we cannot conduct an ANOVA test on price increases. So let’s modify our question:

After COVID (from June 2023 to August 2026) is the average number of price reductions the same across different metro areas, across states?
price_reduced_share: The percent of houses that had price reductions in that metro area
Household Rank: a rank assigned to a metro area the higher number of household the higher the rank (1 being highest)

Null Hypothesis Construction Household Rank

Null Hypothesis \(H_0: \mu_1=\mu_2=...=\mu_{924}=\mu_{925}\) average price reduction share is equal across all household ranks
Alternative Hypothesis \(H_1:\) The 925 mean values are NOT all equal
Alpha \(\alpha=0.05\)

ANOVA Hypothesis Testing Household Rank

anovaRank = aov(price_reduced_share ~ HouseholdRank, data = log_housing)
red_rank_pval = summary(anovaRank)[[1]][1,5]
xkabledply(anovaRank, title = "Price Reduction Share and Household Rank ANOVA result summary")
Price Reduction Share and Household Rank ANOVA result summary
Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
HouseholdRank 924 41.8 0.0453 26.2 0
Residuals 30902 53.3 0.0017 NA NA

Analysis Household Rank

Since our P-value is 0 well below our \(\alpha\) (0.05) we reject our null hypothesis and have data that supports our alternative hypothesis that all average reduction share are not equal across all house ranks.

Of all the 427350 rows in the Tukey test 131817 failed and 295533 passed. That’s 30.845 percent of the pairs failing while 69.155 percent passed. There was also 11446 zero pairs. These problem pairs along with the quick view from our box plotted data confirmed that our results in the ANOVA test having us reject our null hypothesis, but is it the same across states?

Null Hypothesis Construction State

Null Hypothesis \(H_0: \mu_1=\mu_2=...=\mu_{50}=\mu_{51}\) average price reduction share is equal across all sates (and DC)
Alternative Hypothesis \(H_1:\) The 51 mean values are NOT all equal
Alpha \(\alpha=0.05\)

ANOVA Hypothesis Testing State

anovaState = aov(price_reduced_share ~ state_ss, data = log_housing)
red_state_pval = summary(anovaState)[[1]][1,5]
xkabledply(anovaState, title = "Price Reduction Share and State ANOVA result summary")

problem_state_pairs = subset(tukeyStatedf, p.adj<0.05)  # failed
passed_state_pairs = subset(tukeyStatedf, p.adj>=0.05)  # passed

Of all the 1275 rows in the Tukey test 897 failed or 70.353 percent of the pairs failed. While 29.647 percent passed. There was also 356 zero pairs. Within these pairs multiple states are vastly different with others leading to our failed ANOVA test.

Question 3b

After COVID (from June 2023 to August 2026) is the probability that a price increase will happen independent from metro area, from state?
price_increases: a factor which answers if that metro has had any price increases. 0 if price_reduced_share was equal to 0, 1 if it was any higher (denoting that increases did happen).

quality_housing$price_increases = ifelse(quality_housing$price_increased_share == 0, 0, 1)
quality_housing[,51] = as.factor(quality_housing[,51])

EDA

ggplot(quality_housing, aes(fill=price_increases, y=1, x=HouseholdRank)) +

    geom_col(width = 0.5) +

Question 4

After COVID (from June 2023 to August 2026) does the average amount of total listings in a metro area fluctuate during the year? Is there an increase during important times (Ex. start of school/summer)?
total_listing_count: the total amount of listings in that metro area per month

EDA

Let’s first look at the spread of number of total listings (quantitative).

ggplot(data=quality_housing, aes(total_listing_count)) + 
  geom_histogram(breaks=seq(0, 63000, by = 1200), 
                 col="orange", 
                 fill="purple", 
                 alpha = .7) + # opacity
  labs(x="Total Listing Count", y="Frequency") +
  labs(title="Histogram of Total Listing Counts Post COVID")

qqnorm(quality_housing$total_listing_count, main="Q-Q plot of Total Listing Count Post COVID")
qqline(quality_housing$total_listing_count)


Skewed once again let’s normalize and re-plot.

# log transform the data
log_housing$log_list_count = log10(log_housing$total_listing_count + 1)

ggplot(log_housing, aes(x = month_mm, y = log_list_count)) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  geom_boxplot( colour="black", fill="purple", outlier.colour="black", outlier.size=2) +
  labs(title="Boxplot of Month vs Total Listing Count Post COVID", x="month", y = "log10(Total Listing Count)") 

ggplot(data=log_housing, aes(log_list_count)) + 
  geom_histogram(breaks=seq(0, 6, by = 0.2), 
                 col="orange", 
                 fill="purple", 
                 alpha = .7) + # opacity
  labs(x="log10(Total Listing Count)", y="Frequency") +
  labs(title="Histogram of log Total Listing Count Post COVID")

qqnorm(log_housing$log_list_count, main="Q-Q plot of log Total Listing Count Post COVID")
qqline(log_housing$log_list_count)


From the box plots the variability is pretty even among all 12 months (possibly excluding months 1,2, and 12) so the test may fail.

Null Hypothesis Construction Total Listings

Null Hypothesis \(H_0: \mu_1=\mu_2=...=\mu_{11}=\mu_{12}\) average total listing count is equal across all 12 months
Alternative Hypothesis \(H_1:\) The 12 mean values are NOT all equal
Alpha \(\alpha=0.05\)

ANOVA Hypothesis Testing Total Listings

anovaLogList = aov(log_list_count ~ month_mm, data = log_housing)
log_listing_pval = summary(anovaLogList)[[1]][1,5]
xkabledply(anovaLogList, title = "log Total Listing Count and Month ANOVA result summary")
log Total Listing Count and Month ANOVA result summary
Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
month_mm 11 22.1 2.012 5.93 0
Residuals 31815 10789.2 0.339 NA NA

Analysis Total Listings

Since our p-value is 9.8e-10 well below our \(\alpha\) (0.05) we reject our null hypothesis and have data that supports our alternative hypothesis that the average total listing count is not equal across all 12 months.

Post-hoc Tukey Time for Total Listings

tukeyAoVList = TukeyHSD(anovaLogList)

There were only 12 problem pairs of the 66 total pairs or 18.182 percent failed and all of them were either paired with January or February as seen in our box plots. This differs from the initial thought that at the start of school or summer there would be an influx. For the start of school (August & September) there were only 3 failed and 18 passed. That or 14.286 percent failed and 85.714 percent passed. For the start of summer (May & June) there were only 4 failed and 17 passed. That or 19.048 percent failed and 80.952 percent passed.

Key Takeaways

Some limitations of our data was that we don’t know exactly how household rank was calculated so rank may have varied over the different years (this concept was taken into consideration in our earlier questions 1 & 2 but not in 3 & 4). Also for quality this data was stated to be “outside of their typical range, [and] should be reviewed before reporting,” (Realtor.Com Real Estate Data and Market Trends for Download, n.d.) so it was excluded. However, this data could’ve been good data that we just discarded possibly contributing to the skewing in our data. Also the only data we have is on the house itself, data like number of residents or household income aren’t in the report so things like census data could really expand our ability to explore more complex questions.

Overall our data led us to have a better understanding of relationships between price and listing fluctuations based on metro area and time of year. That metro area may play a role when determining things like, price increase/reduction, listing price and counts. Also that pending ratios may have an influence on listing price.
